title: Keeping gains and ending therapy well
summary: For any plan as goals are met: a written staying-well plan, spacing out sessions, booster sessions, and approaches that help prevent a return of depression when there have been earlier episodes.

problems.label: Keeping gains and planning the end of therapy
definitions: Has made progress on the main goals and is starting to talk about spacing out or ending sessions.
Worries that difficulties will come back after therapy ends, or has had earlier periods when they returned.
longTermGoals: The client leaves therapy with a written plan for staying well, knows their early warning signs, and knows how to get help again.

shortTermObjectives.text: In the final 3 sessions, write a short summary with the client of what they learned, the skills that helped most and what to keep practicing.
By the second-to-last session, list at least 3 personal early warning signs and the first 2 steps to take for each, including when to contact the clinician or another service.
Over the last 4 to 8 weeks, space sessions out if the client agrees (for example every 2 weeks, then monthly) and review the chosen measures at each spaced session.
Before the last session, agree whether booster sessions will be offered (for example at 1 and 3 months) and how the client can come back if needed.

When the client has had 2 or more earlier episodes of depression, discuss before ending an approach shown to help prevent a return (for example mindfulness-based cognitive therapy or continued psychological therapy) and any medication plan with the prescriber.
If the client plans to stop a psychiatric medicine, coordinate with the prescriber so that any reduction is planned and monitored, and add its early warning signs to the staying-well plan.

collaborativeNote: Plan the ending with the client from the middle of therapy, not in the last session. The staying-well plan is theirs: use their words for warning signs and steps, and make sure they know how to come back. Do not add names or other identifying details. Resource only. Not a substitute for clinical judgment.
